# Sudden Random Misfire and Stalling RX300

The symptoms you are describing paint a specific picture of an engine that is struggling to maintain closed-loop operation, specifically when transitioning from cold start to operating temperature. The error codes P0300 (random misfire), P0301 (cylinder 1), P0302 (cylinder 2), and P0305 (cylinder 5) suggest a systemic issue rather than an isolated cylinder failure, especially given that cylinders 1 and 2 are adjacent in the front bank.

Your history of maintenanceâreplacing all plugs, PCV valve, intake cleaning, IAC valve, and both coilsâis comprehensive. However, replacing components without addressing underlying vacuum integrity or fuel delivery can sometimes mask a deeper problem temporarily. The fact that the car barely runs when cold but refuses to stay running once it hits closed loop is a classic sign of an air-fuel mixture imbalance under load.

### Evaluating the Vacuum Leak Hypothesis

You attempted to identify a vacuum leak by spraying carburetor cleaner around the intake gaskets and throttle plate. The delayed reaction you observedâ30 to 60 seconds after application leading to a smoothed-out misfire for another 30 secondsâis technically significant but counter-intuitive to standard diagnostic expectations.

Typically, introducing volatile fuel into the intake stream during a vacuum leak test creates an immediate enrichment of the air-fuel mixture. If the engine were running lean due to unmetered air entering through a cracked gasket, you would expect an instant change in idle quality or RPM upon spraying. The delay suggests that the cleaner may not have been reaching the leak directly, or the leak is located downstream of the point you sprayed (e.g., PCV system, brake booster, or fuel pressure regulator vacuum port).

Furthermore, disconnecting the MAF sensor to force the ECU into TPS map mode should theoretically make a vacuum-induced lean condition more pronounced, not less. If the engine ran worse with the throttle applied and didn't improve significantly at idle, it reinforces the idea that the vacuum leak is either negligible or located in a system where the cleaner spray didn't effectively bridge the gap.

### Analyzing O2 Sensor and TPS Data

The observation of significantly different O2 voltages between banks is critical. In a healthy V6 engine, both banks should converge to similar long-term fuel trim values and O2 sensor switching frequencies once closed loop is established. Divergent readings strongly suggest that one bank is running lean (unmetered air) while the other is running correctly, or potentially rich if there is an exhaust leak affecting the upstream sensors.

Regarding your TPS data showing 11% at idle to 75% at WOT without "0 spots": this is likely a display quirk of your Bluetooth OBDII scanner rather than a hardware fault. Most modern TPMS (Throttle Position Sensors) are linear or have a very smooth curve; they do not typically exhibit dead zones in the middle of their range unless there is significant mechanical binding in the throttle body itself. Since you cleaned the intake and IAC, mechanical binding is less likely, but it remains a physical thing worth verifying with a multimeter if the scanner data persists as suspicious.

### Moving to Fuel Delivery Diagnostics

Your suspicion of fuel delivery is well-founded given the pattern of misfires across multiple cylinders, particularly those furthest from the rail (cylinders 1 and 2 in the front bank). While injector clogging or electrical resistance issues are possible, a failing fuel pump or a clogged fuel filter can cause pressure to drop under load when the engine demands more flow.

Connecting a fuel pressure gauge is an excellent next step. You should check both static pressure (key on, engine off) and running pressure (engine idling). More importantly, monitor the pressure while revving the engine to redline. A healthy system should maintain relatively stable pressure; a significant drop indicates a restriction in the supply line or a weak pump.

If your vehicle uses a returnless fuel system common in many Lexus models of this era, pay close attention to the pressure regulator (often located on the rail). If the vacuum line to the regulator is cracked or disconnected, it will cause a lean condition that mimics a vacuum leak but is actually an internal fuel mixture error.

### Final Recommendation

Before you touch the car again, verify the fuel pressure spec for your specific model year. Ensure you have a known good gauge and can read the numbers accurately. If pressure drops significantly under load, inspect the fuel filter next. If pressure holds steady, focus on the divergent O2 sensor data to isolate which bank is starving for air or fuel, as that will direct your inspection toward the intake manifold gaskets specifically affecting the front bank, or potentially an exhaust leak near the catalytic converter.
